newsitem.title: JAPAN: OLYMPICS-WINTER GAMES ORGANISERS ON DEFENSIVE OVER BUREAUCRACY.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-WINTER GAMES ORGANISERS ON DEFENSIVE OVER BUREAUCRACY.

text.p: Japanese organisers of the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics were on the defensive on Monday over a scathing attack on their efforts by the head of their country's own Olympic Committee.

In a Friday meeting with Japanese reporters, Hironoshin Furuhashi, head of the Japanese Olympic Committee, said he had heard "nothing but bad news" about preparations for the games which start in February next year.
"Their (Nagano Olympic Organising Committee - NAOC) way of doing things may or may not be bureaucratic, but it is one-sided," Kyodo News Service quoted Furuhashi as saying.
"If it continues like this, I think the Nagano Games will not be successful."

While Furuhashi, a former Olympic swimmer, Japan ski association chief Yoshiaki Tsutsumi and other top sports officials hold key posts in the organising committee, more than half of NAOC's employees are on loan from Nagano's prefectural and municipal governments.
Others come from the private sector, including NAOC President Eishiro Saito who is a former chairman of the influential Japan Federation of Economic Organisations.
Nagano Prefecture officials defended themselves against charges by Furuhashi that there were too many people among the organisers who were unfamiliar with sports.

"The requests and opinions from the sports federations have not been accepted by NAOC 100 per cent, so they might feel NAOC consists of people who are quite amateur and don't know sports very well," said Mukio Kobayashi, director of the Prefecture's Winter Olympics Division.
"I understand the point, but on the other hand I don't think NAOC can meet every demand from the sports federations," Kobayashi told Reuters.
A NAOC official said the loaned bureaucrats were handling basic administrative preparations for the games, which could make the organising committee appear bureaucratic.
Fumio Watanabe, NAOC deputy director general told Reuters that NAOC's need to maintain a strict budget could also make it appear inflexible.
Sixty-eight events in seven sports, including for the first time snowboarding, curling and women's ice hockey, will be held during the 16-day games beginning on February 7 1998.
NAOC is still embroiled in disputes with skating, Alpine skiing and hockey federations over arrangements for their competitions.
Skating officials are unhappy with hotel accommodation, skiers believe the downhill course is too short and there are complaints that the ice hockey arena is too small for such a popular sport.

"I'm asked by a lot of people whether the Nagano Olympics will turn out okay. If NAOC does not show a more enthusiastic attitude (to improve things), a good mood surrounding the Games will not emerge," Furuhashi said.
Nagano governor Goro Yoshimura became involved last month in a row when he said speed skating was uninteresting as an Olympic event and likened speed skaters to "water beetles on a whirligig."
"Our goal is only to have a successful games," Kobayashi said.
